title: 22. Interview: SLA, SLO, SLI
summary: Interview Q&A for SLA, SLO, SLI — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 SLA, SLO, SLI interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between an SLI, an SLO, and an SLA?
**Answer:** An **SLI** (Service Level Indicator) is the raw measurement — a ratio of good events to total events, like "99.95% of requests returned in < 100 ms." An **SLO** (Service Level Objective) is the target you commit to internally — like "99.9% availability over 28 days." An **SLA** (Service Level Agreement) is the contract with customers — like "99.9% or we refund 10% of your bill." The hierarchy is: SLI (measure) → SLO (internal target) → SLA (external contract). Crucially, the SLA is always *looser* than the SLO, which is always *looser* than actual observed reliability — each layer is a safety buffer. AWS S3's SLA is 99.9% with 10% refund; their internal SLO is much stricter (~99.99%) so they rarely pay credits.
**Visual:**
```
SLI (measure)   : 99.95% of reqs < 100ms
SLO (target)    : 99.9%  over 28 days  (internal)
SLA (contract)  : 99.9%  or refund 10% (external, looser)
ACTUAL          : 99.999% (observed)
```

### Q2. What is an error budget and why is it useful?
**Answer:** The error budget is the inverse of the SLO: a 99.9% SLO over 28 days allows 0.1% × 28 × 24 × 60 = 40.3 minutes of unavailability. The error budget reframes reliability from a binary "is the service up?" to a quantitative "how much unreliability have we consumed?" This allows product and SRE to negotiate rationally: shipping new features consumes budget; when budget is low, releases slow down. Google's SRE practice is explicit — if a team is over budget for two consecutive windows, feature releases are frozen until the budget recovers. Without an error budget, teams either over-invest in reliability (slowing feature velocity) or under-invest (causing outages); with it, the right balance emerges from the data.
**Visual:**
```
SLO 99.9% / 28d = 40.3 min budget
Month 1: 25 min consumed  -> 15 min left -> ship freely
Month 2: 45 min consumed  -> -5 min over -> FREEZE, fix reliability
```

### Q3. How do you choose a good SLI?
**Answer:** A good SLI captures user-perceived outcomes, not protocol-level metrics. Google's recommendation: define SLIs around what users actually experience — latency for interactive requests, throughput for batch, durability for storage, correctness for data processing. The SLI must be a ratio (good/total) measured at the layer users see (load balancer or client SDK, not internal service). A common mistake is choosing an SLI that's easy to measure but doesn't reflect user happiness: "API returned 200" misses the case where it returned 200 in 30 seconds. For a web service, typically two SLIs suffice: availability (success rate) and latency (p99 < threshold). Adding more than 3 SLIs per service is usually a sign the team can't prioritize.
**Visual:**
```
Good SLI:  (reqs with status 2xx/3xx AND latency < 200ms) / total reqs
Bad  SLI:  (reqs with status 2xx/3xx) / total reqs  [ignores latency]
Bad  SLI:  CPU utilization                            [users don't see CPU]
```

### Q4. What is burn rate alerting and why is it better than alerting on the SLO directly?
**Answer:** Alerting on "current 28-day SLO is below target" fires too late — by the time the rolling window dips, you've already consumed the entire budget. Burn rate alerting fires on *how fast* the budget is being consumed. A 14× burn rate means you're consuming a 28-day budget in 2 days — clearly an acute incident. A 3× burn rate means ~9 days to exhaustion — a chronic problem worth a ticket. Google's SRE workbook recommends multi-window alerts: page if 1-hour burn > 14× (acute), ticket if 6-hour burn > 3× (chronic). This catches incidents early without false positives, because a single bad hour is enough to trigger the page while a brief blip doesn't trip the 6-hour window.
**Visual:**
```
Bad:   alert if 28-day SLO < 99.9%   (too late, budget gone)
Good:  page  if 1h burn  >= 14x      (2 days to exhaustion)
       ticket if 6h burn >= 3x       (9 days to exhaustion)
```

### Q5. Why should the SLA always be looser than the SLO?
**Answer:** The SLA is the legal contract that triggers financial consequences (refunds, credits, contract termination). If the SLA equals the SLO, then every internal miss triggers customer-facing penalties — there's no buffer. The standard practice is to make the SLA 10× looser than the SLO: an internal 99.99% SLO maps to a 99.9% SLA. This buffer absorbs bad weeks, regional outages, and operational mistakes without breaching the contract. AWS S3's SLA is 99.9%; their internal SLO is much tighter, so they almost never pay credits. The buffer also lets engineering take calculated risks — a deploy that briefly degrades reliability is fine if it stays well within the SLO-to-SLA gap. Without that gap, every deploy risks contract breach, which freezes release velocity.
**Visual:**
```
Internal SLO: 99.99%   (tight, drives engineering)
External SLA: 99.9%    (10x looser, absorbs bad weeks)
Gap = 0.09% = ~38 min/month buffer for risk-taking
```

### Q6. What is the SRE release-freeze policy and why does it work?
**Answer:** Google's SRE practice: if a team is over its error budget for two consecutive windows (e.g., two consecutive 28-day periods), feature releases are frozen until the budget recovers — only reliability work proceeds. This works because it aligns engineering incentives with user experience: a team that ships features which cause outages loses the right to ship more features until they fix the underlying reliability. The policy is quantitative (driven by the error budget) rather than political, which removes the "should we ship?" debate. The threat of release freeze motivates teams to invest in test coverage, canary deploys, and rollback automation *before* the budget runs out. The unfreeze happens automatically when the budget recovers, which keeps the policy objective rather than punitive.
**Visual:**
```
Window 1: budget exhausted (over)        -> warning
Window 2: budget exhausted again (over)  -> FREEZE releases
                                       -> only reliability work
Budget recovers to >50%               -> UNFREEZE, ship again
```

### Q7. How do you measure an SLI in practice?
**Answer:** Instrument your code with OpenTelemetry or Prometheus. For availability, increment two counters: `requests_total` and `requests_success_total`; the SLI is `success / total` over the window. For latency, use a histogram (Prometheus `Histogram`, OpenTelemetry `Histogram`) bucketed at the SLO thresholds (e.g., 50ms, 100ms, 200ms, 500ms, 1s) so you can compute p99 from the bucket counts — counters can't give percentiles. Measure at the layer users see: for an HTTP service, the load balancer or API gateway, not an internal microservice. For mobile apps, instrument the client SDK so you capture network failures the server never sees. Export to your observability backend (Prometheus, Datadog, Honeycomb) and compute the SLI as a query (`sum(rate(requests_success_total[28d])) / sum(rate(requests_total[28d]))`). Critical: validate that "success" matches user-perceived success — a 200 with a slow body or empty response is not a success.
**Visual:**
```
Counter:  requests_total{status="200"}    -> 1,000,000
          requests_success_total          ->   999,500  (200 + < 200ms)
SLI = 999500 / 1000000 = 99.95%   vs SLO 99.9%   -> within budget

Histogram: http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.2"} -> 999,500
                                            {le="+Inf"} -> 1,000,000
p99 latency -> bucket containing 99th percentile
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 28 days. On day 5, a 30-minute outage occurs. How much budget is left and what should you do?
**Answer:** Budget = 0.1% × 28 × 24 × 60 = 40.3 minutes. The 30-minute outage consumes 30 minutes, leaving 10.3 minutes (25% remaining) for the remaining 23 days. That's a 0.45 min/day remaining burn rate, which is very tight — any further outage will blow the budget. Actions: (1) publish the budget status to the team so everyone knows we're tight; (2) freeze risky feature releases for the next 2 weeks (release only bug fixes and reliability work); (3) run a blameless postmortem on the 30-minute outage and implement the action items; (4) add canary deploys and automated rollback to prevent similar incidents; (5) consider pre-scaling (Topic 13) and additional load testing (Topic 14) for the next peak window. If a second incident consumes the remaining 10 minutes, the SLO is breached — that's when the release freeze becomes mandatory for the rest of the window.
**Visual:**
```
Day 5: 30-min outage -> budget 40.3 - 30 = 10.3 min (25% left)
       freeze releases, postmortem, canary deploys, pre-scale
Day 6-28: monitor closely, budget only allows ~0.45 min/day
```

### Q2. Your team proposes a 99.99% availability SLO for a new internal service. Is this reasonable?
**Answer:** Probably not. 99.99% over 28 days = 4.0 minutes of allowed unavailability per window. For an *internal* service (no external SLA, no customer refunds), this is over-engineered — the team will spend disproportionate effort on reliability at the expense of feature velocity, and one bad deploy will blow the budget. The right approach: (1) derive the SLO from downstream user needs — what availability do the *consumers* of this service actually need? If they're internal tools used during business hours, 99.5% (84 min/week allowed) is likely fine; (2) start with a looser SLO (99.5% or 99.9%) and tighten only if downstream users complain; (3) measure current performance — if it's 99.6%, setting SLO at 99.99% sets an unrealistic target that just demoralizes the team. Google's rule of thumb: most internal services should target 99.9% or 99.95%; reserve 99.99%+ for critical-path user-facing services.
**Visual:**
```
Internal service 99.99% = 4 min/28d -> over-engineered
Better: 99.9% (40 min/28d) or 99.5% (5h/28d) depending on downstream needs
Reserve 99.99%+ for: checkout, auth, payments -> external, SLA-backed
```

### Q3. Your service is consistently running at 99.999% (much better than the 99.9% SLO). What should you do?
**Answer:** Counterintuitively, this is a problem. You're over-investing in reliability at the expense of feature velocity — the team is being too conservative, deploying slowly, over-provisioning capacity, and avoiding risk. The SRE answer: relax the SLO. Move from 99.9% to 99.5% (or wherever the actual user pain threshold is), which gives you a much larger error budget and lets the team ship faster, take more risks, and reduce cost (smaller fleet, less redundancy). The error budget is a *resource* to be spent on innovation, not a metric to be hoarded. Concretely: (1) analyze user behavior to find the actual pain threshold (when do users churn? when do support tickets spike?); (2) set the SLO just below that threshold; (3) communicate to the team that they're now encouraged to take calculated risks (canary more aggressively, deploy more often, accept brief latency spikes during deploys). Google explicitly does this — many of their services have been *relaxed* over time as the team matured.
**Visual:**
```
Actual 99.999% >> SLO 99.9%:    over-invested, slow velocity
Relax SLO to 99.5%:             bigger budget, ship faster, cut cost
Goal: actual ~ SLO + small buffer, not actual >> SLO
```

### Q4. You're alerted at 02:00 with "1-hour burn rate 14×". The service is up and serving traffic. What do you do?
**Answer:** Don't dismiss the alert — burn rate alerts fire on user-perceived failures, not on service-down events. The 14× burn rate means you're consuming 14× the normal error rate, which could be: (1) elevated latency past the SLO threshold (responses are slow but returning 200); (2) elevated 5xx errors on a small fraction of requests; (3) a partial outage affecting one AZ or one user segment; (4) a slow degradation that hasn't yet crossed a "service down" threshold. Action: (1) check the SLI dashboard for the specific SLI burning (availability vs latency); (2) check recent deploys — was there a deploy in the last hour? If so, rollback is the fastest fix; (3) check downstream dependencies for saturation; (4) check error logs for new error types; (5) if you can't find the cause in 10 minutes, page the broader team — a 14× burn will exhaust the budget in 2 days, but the *user impact* may already be significant. Document the investigation in the incident channel.
**Visual:**
```
02:00: 1h burn = 14x -> PAGE
02:01: SLI dashboard -> which SLI? latency p99 spiking?
02:02: recent deploy? -> yes, 01:45 -> ROLLBACK
02:05: rollback complete -> burn rate drops -> resolve alert
```

### Q5. A customer demands a 99.99% SLA in their contract. Your internal SLO is 99.95%. What do you do?
**Answer:** Do not sign the contract as-is. The SLA should always be 10× looser than the internal SLO — if you promise 99.99% externally while targeting 99.95% internally, you'll be paying service credits constantly. Three options: (1) **negotiate the SLA down** to 99.9% (10× looser than your 99.95% SLO is actually 99.95%, but standard practice is to round down for safety); (2) **invest in raising the SLO** to 99.995%+ so the 99.99% SLA fits the 10× buffer principle — this requires multi-AZ active-active (Topic 13), canary deploys (Topic 14), and rigorous error budget tracking; (3) **offer tiered SLAs** — 99.9% standard, 99.99% for a premium tier with higher pricing that funds the additional reliability work. Option 2 is the right answer for strategically important customers but requires significant engineering investment (3-6 months for a typical service). Be transparent with the customer: explain the buffer principle, share the roadmap to 99.99% SLO, and offer interim credits if the SLA is breached during the ramp-up.
**Visual:**
```
Customer wants:  99.99% SLA
Current SLO:     99.95%   (only 0.05% buffer -> breach risk high)
Options:
  A) Negotiate SLA to 99.9% (10x looser than 99.95% SLO)
  B) Invest SLO -> 99.995%, then SLA 99.99% (3-6 months eng)
  C) Tiered: 99.9% standard, 99.99% premium ($$$)
```

### Q6. Your SLI dashboard shows 99.95% availability, but the SLO is 99.9% — you're under budget. Yet customer complaints are rising. What's wrong?
**Answer:** Classic SLI/user-perception mismatch. The SLI is measuring the wrong thing. Likely culprits: (1) **measuring at the wrong layer** — your SLI is at the application, but users are seeing LB failures or DNS issues that the app never sees; (2) **counting bad responses as good** — your SLI counts any 2xx as success, but 200-with-empty-body or 200-with-slow-TTFB is a failure for users; (3) **averaging over the wrong window** — the 28-day rolling average hides recent acute incidents that are still fresh in users' minds; (4) **ignoring latency** — availability is 99.95% but p99 latency is 10 seconds, so users perceive the service as broken; (5) **bias in measurement** — synthetic probes from your VPC see different behavior than real users on mobile networks. Fix: (1) measure at the client SDK layer (mobile apps, browser) to capture what users actually see; (2) redefine "good" to require both 2xx AND latency under threshold; (3) break the SLI down by user segment (region, device, network) to find which users are seeing problems; (4) add a second SLI for latency p99. Re-validate the SLI against complaint volume; if complaints persist while SLI looks healthy, the SLI is wrong.
**Visual:**
```
Bad  SLI: 200 / total        -> 99.95%  (users complain)
Good SLI: (200 AND <200ms) / total  -> reveals true user pain
Measure at: client SDK > LB > app  (closest to user wins)
Segment by: region, device, network -> find unhappy users
```

### Q7. Your team has 12 SLIs across one service. Each has its own SLO and alert. The on-call is drowning in pages. How do you fix this?
**Answer:** 12 SLIs is a red flag — Google recommends 1-3 per user-facing service. The team can't prioritize, alerting is noisy, and the error budgets are meaningless because each SLI has its own budget (no unified signal). Action plan: (1) **audit the SLIs** — for each, ask: does it capture a distinct user-perceived outcome? Is it on the critical user path? Most will fail this test (e.g., CPU utilization, queue depth, log volume are *operational metrics*, not user-facing SLIs); (2) **consolidate to 2-3 user-facing SLIs** — typically availability (success rate) and latency (p99) for the critical user journey (e.g., "checkout succeeds in < 500 ms"); (3) **move operational metrics to dashboards and saturation alerts** — alert on CPU > 80% as a saturation warning, not as an SLO breach; (4) **unify the error budget** — combine the 2-3 SLIs into one composite budget (e.g., "SLO is met if both availability AND latency SLOs are met"); (5) **set burn-rate alerts on the unified budget** — page on acute burn, ticket on chronic. Result: 3-5 alerts per service instead of 30, and the team knows exactly what user outcome they're protecting.
**Visual:**
```
Before: 12 SLIs (CPU, mem, queue, FD, log vol, 4xx, 5xx, p50, p90, p99, ...) -> 30 alerts/page
After:  2 user-facing SLIs (availability + p99 latency)
          + composite error budget
          + 2 burn-rate alerts (page + ticket)
        + saturation dashboard for ops metrics
```
